Subject: Redwood Dedicated eval & capacity guarantees — follow-up + next steps

Thanks for the call this morning — good to learn more about Fintech.io's latency-sensitive fraud-scoring use case and the expected growth profile (peak windows with sustained throughput needs). Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have alignment: 

Call recap:
- Primary objective: replace current hyperscaler on-demand inference for fraud scoring with a predictable, lower-cost serving platform that meets p99 latency targets during peak windows and provides capacity guarantees.
- Key constraints: data residency in us-west, strict audit trail for inference requests, and long-tail batches at 1.5–2k tokens.
- Current environment: mixed multi-model workloads, currently using GCP Vertex + preemptible instances for cost control; spikes have resulted in throttling and degraded p99s.

How Redwood Dedicated maps to your needs (high level):
1) Reserved GPU pools with capacity guarantees — customers reserve dedicated node pools (GPU-backed) that we operate for them. That gives predictable throughput and avoids preemption/eviction issues you saw with preemptible instances.
2) SLA-backed latency & availability targets for Dedicated plans — we can include p99 latency targets and uptime in the SOW for reserved capacity.
3) Smart routing + autoscaling buffers — Dedicated supports configurable burst capacity and automatic fallback to compatible model variants if there's unexpected demand, minimizing dropped requests.
4) Observability & auditability — token-level cost/latency breakdown, request tracing, and audit logs for compliance.
5) Model/runtime optimizations — our serving runtime supports continuous batching, KV caching, and quantization profiles to reduce cost while meeting latency SLOs.

Competitive framing vs hyperscalers (summary):
- Hyperscaler reserved instances (EC2/GCE): lower friction for infra teams but limited inference stack (you still manage model serving, batching, and fallback logic). Instance reservation covers capacity but not the application-level SLOs or inference optimizations. Risk: you pay for reserved instances and still need engineering effort to reach target p99.
- Hyperscaler managed inference APIs: easy to get started but limited visibility into kernel selection, batching, and caching; pricing and throttling policies can be opaque at scale.
- Redwood Dedicated: provides an opinionated inference runtime + reserved capacity + SLOs. We take on operational responsibility for inference (patching, kernel tuning, autoscaling policies) and tie capacity to SLOs in the contract.

Proposed next steps (recommended):
1) SE call (30–45m) with Rajiv + Sean to review the exact traffic profile and test plan (I copied Sean on this thread).
2) 72-hour dedicated performance run: we provision a small dedicated pool (config below) and run a controlled workload to capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cost.
3) SOW + pricing: I attached a short PoC SOW template and a slide that compares Dedicated vs hyperscaler approaches.

Proposed test config (to discuss on SE call):
- Model: customer-provided transformer (we can also test with an open LLM baseline)
- Pool: 2 nodes (A100-class equivalent), pinned to us-west region, no preemption
- Traffic: synthetic replay of your peak window (target sustained concurrency ~200 requests, 2k token typical).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, error rate, and token cost.

Please review the attached slides and SOW. If that plan looks good, propose two time slots for the SE call this week — I can book Sean and our infra lead Dev.

Thanks — Marissa

Thanks Marissa — this is helpful. A few clarifying questions before we lock the SE call: 

1) Network / egress: does Redwood Dedicated require traffic to egress through your hosted control plane for inference, or can traffic remain fully within our VPC with private peering? We need to avoid cross-region egress costs.
2) Data residency + audit logs: the audit logs you mentioned — are those delivered to our logging stack (we use Splunk) and retained for 90 days by default? Can retention be extended?
3) Benchmarks vs GCP Vertex: our infra team would like a direct apples-to-apples comparison vs the Vertex AI inference offering using the same model and tokens. How do you ensure fairness of the test (kernel/quantization differences)?
4) Pricing model for reserved pools: are we billed on a monthly committed spend or on consumed tokens on top of the reserved node fee? What's the minimum commit term?

If you can answer the above in-thread we can prep Rajiv and the infra folks. We are available for an SE call Thursday 2/19 10:00–11:30 PT or Friday 2/20 14:00–16:00 PT — whichever works for your team.

—Olivia

Olivia — thanks for the quick questions. Answers inline below, plus proposed next steps and times.

1) Network / egress:
- Redwood Dedicated supports private peering (VPC peering / private link) so inference traffic can remain on your network fabric in us-west — no public internet egress required. That also lets us avoid cross-region egress charges if the pool is in the same region. We'll document the peering steps in the SOW and run a short network validation during the initial provisioning.

2) Data residency + audit logs:
- Audit logs: we stream structured audit events to customer-provided endpoints (Splunk/Datadog/S3) using your ingestion token. Default retention is 90 days in our managed log store; we can export to your Splunk with configurable retention for longer dwell. We'll include the delivery method and retention options in the SOW.

3) Fair benchmarking vs GCP Vertex:
- We'll run an apples-to-apples test: same model weights or agreed open baseline, same tokenizer, and identical request traces replayed against both platforms. To address kernel/quantization differences, we'll test two setups: (a) nominal fp16 baseline on both platforms, (b) a quantized run reflecting what you would run in production. We'll report per-run configuration details so the comparison is reproducible. SE call will cover exact measurement harness.

4) Pricing model for reserved pools:
- Billing model: two components — (1) reserved node fee (monthly pro-rated for POC) which guarantees capacity, and (2) usage-based token compute on top if you exceed baseline thresholds (this is optional depending on how the SOW is structured). Minimum commit term: quarterly for Dedicated, but for POCs we can do a short-term billed trial (72-hour or 30-day) with a small refundable credit/PO. I'll surface any discount possibilities after we sync on scope.

Proposed immediate next steps:
- SE call: Thu 2/19 10:30–11:15 PT (we'll confirm availability for Sean & Dev) OR Fri 2/20 14:00–14:45 PT. Please confirm which slot works for Rajiv + infra.
- If SE call looks good, we'll: (a) finalize test config, (b) provision a small Dedicated pool, (c) run a 72-hour test and share detailed results + cost estimation.

Attached: updated slide comparing Dedicated vs hyperscaler plus a short SOW and SLA overview.

Would you like me to send a brief one-page comparison (2–3 bullets per row) vs Vertex and EC2 reserved instances to share with your infra and procurement teams? Happy to do that.

Best — Marissa
